ASRSN:2176000.n: When planning the flight into TSP, the NOTAM revealed several taxiways that were closed. The day of the flight, we attempted to contact the airport authority. It was Day 0 and the airport authority did not answer the phone, however, the Tehachapi police department answered the call. They had no knowledge of the airfield situation.The notes revealed several taxiways that were closed, and upon reviewing the Tehachapi plates, there was only one plate for the airfield diagram, as there are no approaches to the runway. The airfield diagram plate only showed the runway and taxiways, but no taxiway designators. That is why we wanted to contact the airfield authority to determine the suitability of the field.We launched for Tehachapi and overflew the airport and viewed the construction and determined it was safe to land.Upon clearing the runway, we noticed that down the parallel taxiway they had orange cones on the right side and on the left side, they had new taxiway designators that were fixed as it all airports.We slowly taxi down the parallel taxiway, and the cones were extremely close to the wing however, they were lower than the wing itself as were the taxiway designators taxi into parking and when we left, we chose a different route to get to the runway for departure.In light of the inability to talk to airfield personnel, I would highly recommend we do not use Tehachapi airport until all of the construction is complete. There are just too many hazardous areas to navigate around, and without adequate reference to taxiways on the only airfield diagram that does not have taxiway designation, I recommend we suspend operations into TSP until construction is complete.Cause: Lack of ability to talk to airport personnel and an inadequate airfield diagram that identifies taxiways.Suggestions: Better communications with airport personnel, especially during construction operations.
ASRSN:2176000.s: The flight crew encountered closed taxiways and an inadequate airfield diagram at Tehachapi (TSP) while unable to contact airport personnel. After visually confirming safety, they landed but faced narrow taxiing clearance due to construction cones, prompting a recommendation to suspend operations until construction completes.

ASRSN:2176003.n: While flying the ANTHM4 arrival into BWI, we were descending through 11,800 approximately 5 miles from the JABRR fix, when I pulled the airspeed knob and selected 250 KIAS. The aircraft slightly pitched up and slowed its descent to facilitate the slowdown. When it reached 250 KIAS, we were descending through approximately 11,300' MSL, two miles prior to the fix. The nose then lowered and the aircraft settled into a 1500 FPM descent with no sign of leveling at the hard-coded altitude restriction of 11,000. I intervened and leveled the airplane manually at 11,000. Then, once we had passed the fix, I re-entered NAV mode, with no further issues on the arrival. It is important to note that I have flown this arrival three times in the past two weeks, in three different nose numbers, and I have replicated this behavior EACH TIME, exactly as described here.
ASRSN:2176003.s: During the ANTHM4 arrival into BWI, the pilot reported that after selecting 250 KIAS, the aircraft failed to level at the 11,000-foot restriction at JABRR, requiring manual intervention. The pilot noted this behavior occurred consistently across three different aircraft in the past two weeks.

ASRSN:2176022.n: We experienced several MX (Maintenance) issues during climb out and then ultimately at cruise enroute from ZZZ to ZZZ1. First issue was a flight control issue we noticed during our multiple level offs during our climb up to cruise. We noted that the plane was flying with a roughly 3 degree turn of roll to the right while in level flight. We tried to rectify the issue by cycling the autopilot and hand flying but the issue remained. The CA (Captain) started a discussion with Maintenance Control and Dispatch to write up the issue. While we worked problem 1 problem 2 emerged. The number 2 brake temp sensor started to behave erratically and was giving us an intermittent hot brakes ECAM and was showing brake temps up to 900C, before the sensor displayed XX and stopped providing input. We discussed our options and contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control. After working on problem 2 we got another ECAM for Door R Aft EMER Exit. This ECAM has the crew monitor cabin pressure and if necessary perform an emergency descent down to 10,000 ft. After discussing this third problem with Maintenance Control and Dispatch the CA decided to change our destination to ZZZ2 in order to have MX look at the plane. I contacted ATC and notified them of our intentions to change our destination, and that we were not [requesting priority handling]. We chose a lower altitude and then had an uneventful return to ZZZ after Dispatch asked us to fly there instead of ZZZ2. We landed at ZZZ and handed the plane back off to MX.
ASRSN:2176022.s: The crew encountered flight control, brake sensor, and emergency exit door issues during climb and cruise from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After consulting Maintenance Control and Dispatch, they diverted to ZZZ2, then returned to ZZZ at a lower altitude to hand the aircraft to maintenance.

ASRSN:2176062.n: Prior to brake release we received the final Dangerous Goods (DG) summary. The FO sent the DG acknowledgement code via ACARS and we received the confirmation message. After brake release an ACARS message that we must acknowledge final DG. On the printer was a second final DG with the DG offloaded. We sent a second DG acknowledgement code via ACARS.
ASRSN:2176062.s: The flight crew received a second final Dangerous Goods summary after brake release indicating offloaded items. They sent a second acknowledgement code via ACARS to confirm the updated manifest.

ASRSN:2176063.n: The Tower Controller for my runway is transmitting ONLY on the Tower frequency for the runway I am using. The Monitor frequency is being used/transmitted on by another Controller, working either a different runway or a different part of the airport operation. I am getting two Controllers talking over each other, complete with taxi/hold short/other instructions for a different runway in a different voice and simultaneously with instructions on my primary frequency. To be clear: I was cleared for the ILS PRM approach, not the regular ILS.This is NOT an isolated incident. I have seen this on multiple occasions - of course over several years since PRMs aren't that common and I don't get to ORD that often.
ASRSN:2176063.s: A pilot conducting an ILS PRM approach at ORD reported hearing two controllers transmit simultaneously on the primary and monitor frequencies. This overlap caused conflicting taxi and hold short instructions for different runways to be heard at the same time.

ASRSN:2176069.n: Holding short of Taxiway U on Bravo Line North. Received taxi clearance to turn right on to Taxiway G. Turned on taxi light and was moving 3-5 knots and about to cross the painted access road between Terminal C and Terminal B, when a tug pulling a baggage cart moving from Terminal C to Terminal B drove in front of the aircraft.
ASRSN:2176069.s: While taxiing at 3-5 knots from Taxiway U to G, a tug pulling a baggage cart drove in front of the aircraft as it approached the access road between Terminals C and B. The incident occurred after the pilot received clearance and activated the taxi light.

ASRSN:2176075.n: On approach into ZZZ XXL we were last given a vector about 350 at 4000 ft. Two or 3 miles north of ZZZZZ's we were cleared the visual. The PM asked if I wanted flaps 10, set them after I said yes, rolled in a lower altitude (I can't remember what) and tried to engage VNAV. As the pitch mode entered V/S I continued the descent while turning to final. I asked for Gear and FLAPS 15 as we turned out on final and around 2000 ft I asked what altitude we needed to be at. The PM checked his plate and said climb. Shortly after tower advised us that we were low and the PM responded we were in the climb. We intercepted the correct glide path shortly after and made an uneventful landing. ZZZZZ Arrival to Visual XXL. On 140 vector out of ZZZZZ1, given descent to 4,000 ft followed by a left turn 330 outside of ZZZZZ2. Vector flew through path of ZZZZ ZZZ RNAV course, which was loaded into the box. While aircrew were cycling DXXXL to the top of the LEGS page, approach issued traffic twelve o'clock for Runway XXR, maintain visual separation, cleared visual Runway XXL, contact tower XXX.X". Crew read back, "#, maintain visual separation with traffic to Runway XXR, cleared visual Runway XXL, switching tower XXX.X." Approach requested another full read back to include "Aircraft X;" which we compiled with, "Aircraft X #, maintain visual separation with traffic to Runway XXR, cleared visual Runway XXL, switching tower XXX.X." 1800 ft was entered into the altitude window for DXXXL, however VNAV was not available. EXEC had not been selected earlier when sequencing DXXXL due to the traffic call and back and forth on the clearance read back. ZZZZZ2 (5000 ft) and ZZZZZ (4100 ft) remained in LEGS page, which inhibited VNAV, since the airplane was at 4000 ft in ALT HOLD. Therefore the aircraft went into V/S descent when 1800 ft was selected. In this process, crew misidentified the field visually and began a descent. As the box was cleaned up to sequence DXXXL, aircrew noted that they were below the 2700 ft altitude at DXXXL and initiated a climb to comply with charted altitude guidance. As tower was selected into the radio, tower stated, Aircraft X #, low altitude, initiate climb, altimeter 30.07." Aircrew replied with , "Aircraft X # is in a climb, 30.07, Visual Runway XXL." Landing clearance was given and the remainder of the approach and landing were flown without issue. Though the intention was to use VNAV protection for the descent, an errant missing of an EXEC command due to distraction rendered VNAV unavailable. Combined with the expectation of always being high in ZZZ and needing to configure early, the aircrew had a confirmation bias that a descent was needed as the box was cleaned up."
ASRSN:2176075.s: The flight crew descended below the required 2700 ft during a visual approach to Runway XXL after failing to execute the FMS, which inhibited VNAV and caused an unintended V/S descent. Tower alerted them to the low altitude, prompting an immediate climb to intercept the glide path for a safe landing.

ASRSN:2176085.n: We were flying the Tip Toe Visual 28L with traffic on 28R converging as they were lining up with their centerline. The crosswind out of the North was 30-35 kts. Approaching 1300' we received a TCAS alert followed shortly by a TCAS RA. The intruder was slightly above us on our right side, my FO had him visually and we were directed to descend. Approaching 1000' the RA stopped and simultaneously Tower called with a low level altitude alert. The FO responded with TCAS RA. We were approximately 1.5 dots below GS, visual over water with no obstacles. I corrected toward GS and we were stabilized above 500' RA and elected to land. The landing was uneventful. On the Tipp Toe Visual 28L we got a 'descend' TCAS RA at approximately 1400' followed by 'monitor vertical speed' for Aircraft Y on the parallel visual approach. The Captain was hand flying and responded to the RA initially and reduced the decent passing through 1000'. I had the traffic insight during the whole event. We were stabilized on the approach after the RA by 700'. We elected to continue the approach due to being stable and not wanting to climb for a go around causing a subsequent RA after the 'descend' RA.
ASRSN:2176085.s: Pilots on a parallel visual approach to runway 28L received a TCAS 'descend' RA at 1400 feet due to traffic on runway 28R. They reduced descent, stabilized above 500 feet, and completed an uneventful landing after electing to continue rather than climb for a go-around.

ASRSN:2176111.n: During cruise flight at 31,000 ft near the ZZZZZ intersection, the left IRS (Inertial Reference System) failed. The plane abruptly turned and dove about 400 ft before I got manual control of it and returned to course & altitude. The FO was just returning from the lav. When he was settled, I asked him to fly while I ran the QRH. We informed ATC of our nav issue and apologized for the temporary altitude deviation.Cause was left IRS failure. No recommendations to mitigate.
ASRSN:2176111.s: During cruise at 31,000 ft near ZZZZZ, a left IRS failure caused the aircraft to turn and dive 400 ft. The captain regained manual control, the First Officer flew while the captain ran the QRH, and ATC was informed of the deviation.

ASRSN:2176163.n: On our climb out, we got a report to look for traffic at our 3 O'Clock position. My First Officer advised me that he couldn't see the traffic do to his window having several scratches which obstructed his view for locating our traffic. Local Maintenance told me that if it was within limits he was going to sign it off. This is a safety issue due to the inability to locate our traffic because you cannot effectively see out the window because of the severity of the scratches.
ASRSN:2176163.s: During climb out, the First Officer could not locate traffic at 3 O'clock due to severe window scratches obstructing his view. Local Maintenance indicated they would sign off the damage if within limits, but the crew reported this as a safety issue preventing effective traffic detection.

ASRSN:2176205.n: Climbing through FL280 ECAM Air Eng Bleed 1, began procedure, then Eng 2 bleed ECAM followed immediately with APU bleed leak. Leveled around FL290 [advised ATC] and return to ZZZ and began descent. Landing uneventful in ZZZ. While climbing through approximately FL280, we received an ECAM for AIR ENG 1 BLEED LEAK. While responding to the ECAM, it was noticed that we also had a AIR ENG 2 BLEED LEAK and APU BLEED LEAK. [We advised ATC] and clearance back to ZZZ was requested. The ECAM was actioned and an uneventful return and landing at ZZZ was accomplished.
ASRSN:2176205.s: During climb through FL280, the crew received simultaneous ECAM warnings for Engine 1, Engine 2, and APU bleed leaks. They leveled at FL290, advised ATC, and returned to ZZZ for an uneventful landing after completing the required procedures.

ASRSN:2176211.n: We were on a visual approach to 14 in RAP. FO decided to hand fly. He turned off the automation and turned a tight base leg. As we joined the final approach course, I quickly realized we were very high. He attempted to do a slight S-turn. I told him it was not going to work and to prepare to go around. A few seconds later I told him we are way too high, let's go around". The FO wanted to do a 360 degree turn instead to lose altitude. I called Tower requesting a 360. There was not a response. I radioed Tower again, he did not respond. I looked down at the audio panel and the frequency on the plate thinking I may have accidentally switched it when I put Ground in standby. When I looked up, the FO had put us in a quick right turn. I told him "you cannot do this without clearance." And instructed him to re-join the final. He told me he was cleared for the visual and did not need a clearance. As he brought the wing level to turn back, I again requested clearance to do the maneuver from the controller as we were now off of the final course. I then called for a go around again. Simultaneously, we received the clearance to perform a 360 degree turn. The FO immediately continued the right turn. We rejoined the final at traffic pattern altitude. While back on final, a little under 1000 feet AGL, the FO received a "sink rate" warning as he was correcting from getting high on the approach due to a high thrust setting from the 360 degree turn. I called out the excessive sink rate. The FO added additional power and raised the nose and stabilized on the PAPIs. In hindsight, without a doubt, I should have commanded a go around and stuck with my decision. I realize now that I had initially "casually instructed" the go around as part of a sentence. However, I think the FO did not register the call as I included it within a sentence and he was overwhelmed with the airplane. When we de-briefed, the FO did not recall being told to go around either time. My instruction should have been standalone and clear. Once the decision was made, I should not have reconsidered. Additionally, I should have taken control of the aircraft when he became unresponsive to the go around instruction. I am kicking myself over and over about even entertaining the 360 degree turn. I've never permitted something like this before. This was thoroughly debriefed. Additionally, we thoroughly debriefed what are acceptable maneuvers when cleared for a visual approach in controlled airspace. After our de-brief, the FO understood why he needed an ATC clearance to perform a 360 degree turn maneuver. Additionally, we de-briefed a visual approach set up from the downwind. We discussed the SOP/recommended technique for configuration timing and spacing on visual approaches. When I got to the hotel, I wrote a report and de-briefed the event with a review team. After our de-brief, the FO and I sat down the next day and we de-briefed some additional points."
ASRSN:2176211.s: During a visual approach to Runway 14, the First Officer flew a tight base leg and executed an unauthorized 360-degree turn, causing the aircraft to become high and trigger a sink rate warning. The Captain attributed the incident to unclear go-around commands and the First Officer's failure to recognize the need for ATC clearance for the maneuver.

ASRSN:2176230.n: Encountered wake turbulence on short final which led to an unstable approach. Performed a normal go-around and landed uneventfully.
ASRSN:2176230.s: The pilot encountered wake turbulence on short final, causing an unstable approach. A normal go-around was performed, resulting in an uneventful landing.

ASRSN:2176239.n: Taking off from RWY XX at ZZZ approximately 90 kts. the main cabin door light illuminated. I rejected the T/O. FO let the Tower know and followed SOP. We taxied off the RWY and ran the Rejected QRC. Found we needed 36 minutes in the brake cooling chart. I talked the Purser and she said everyone was okay. I called Dispatch and Maintenance Control. We decided to take the airplane back to the gate. I informed the passengers and we then taxied back to the gate. The plane was taken out of service to investigate the door.
ASRSN:2176239.s: The flight crew rejected takeoff at 90 knots from RWY XX at ZZZ after the main cabin door light illuminated. Following the Rejected QRC and confirming passenger safety, the aircraft was returned to the gate and taken out of service for door investigation.

ASRSN:2176241.n: Because of weather and airspace changes we were high enough at 4 miles from the FAF to ask Tower for a left 360 at 4200 feet in VMC at night. There was no way we would make the decent to runway 11 and be stable. We asked for and received clearance for a left 360 from Tower. We started a left 360 while still descending and I verbally stated that the MSA was 6000 as we were handed back off to Approach Control by Tower. They informed us that they couldn't give us terrain clearance and said continue at our own risk.I immediately disconnected the autopilot and started a right turn back toward the final while initiating a climb when I realized our terrain clearance wouldn't be enough for the 360. I then told the FO to ask for a heading and altitude. We then established the aircraft back on a safe path away from the terrain. ATC asked if we could land the opposite runway, 29, and we agreed with calm winds and set up for the approach and landing.No other issues occurred and we landed without incident.
ASRSN:2176241.s: The crew requested a left 360 at 4,200 feet due to weather but was denied terrain clearance by Approach Control. The pilot immediately climbed and turned right to avoid terrain, then accepted a clearance to land on the opposite runway, 29, without incident.

ASRSN:2176250.n: We were cleared to cross 4L on Y contact ramp control. After we were cleared tower cleared a regional jet to cross on W. We called ramp tower and we were cleared to the gate via Y and Taxiway 1 to the gate. When the regional jet got cleared U A Taxiway 2 to the gate they were just passing us on W. I asked the FO if anyone was told to give way he did not know so had him ask controller to clarify instructions. By this point the regional jet started its turn onto U obviously not waiting for us to pass. I had time to give way to the regional jet because I thought he might make the turn in front of us and had slowed to prevent an accident. Had I not known the taxiways and listened to his clearance we would have hit with serious damage. The ramp tower controller said they did not control Y and W so it was grounds fault. They gave the clearance in and should have been responsible for the separation of aircraft.
ASRSN:2176250.s: The pilot and a regional jet experienced a near collision while taxiing on Y and W after conflicting clearances from ramp and tower controllers. The pilot slowed to avoid the jet, attributing the incident to the controllers' failure to manage separation on the taxiways they cleared.

ASRSN:2176263.n: Descending on the PHLBO arrival somewhere SOMTO, we were given turn right 090 and maintain 8000'". Few minutes later we thought we heard "cleared direct DOOIN" so we entered that and went into LNAV. Couple minutes later approach asked if we were on the arrival and we said "no, you cleared us direct DOOIN". approach said "no I didn't but just go direct GRITTY and join the localizer". They mentioned they gave us direct DYLIN. We were instructed to fly on a heading a good bit off the arrival and going down to 8k or maybe even 5k feet at this point so we both initially head DOOIN. I think the initial was how close DYLIN and DOOIN sounds and being that far off the arrival with EWR landing north, we figured he said DOOIN. I think next time, we will verify with them which point they want when points sound that close to each other." ATC issued us a heading and an altitude below the bottom altitude of the PHLBO arrival. The next clearance was to proceed direct DOINN. ATC then questioned whether or not we were on the arrival. I stated no that we were direct DOINN. ATC then stated he wanted us to go to DYLIN, bit then amended the route to direct GRITY. Approaches final comment was ok no big deal." we proceeded without further incident."
ASRSN:2176263.s: Pilots descending on the PHLBO arrival misheard a clearance for DYLIN as DOOIN due to similar names, causing them to deviate from the arrival. ATC corrected the route to GRITTY, and the flight continued without incident after the crew acknowledged the need to verify similar-sounding waypoints.

ASRSN:2176306.n: Passengers on the ZZZ1 flight had a rideable carry-on bag. The first thing I did was call up to Security and I spoke to Person A to let him know the situation. I asked him if I should file a report and he said there's no need and that he'll notify ZZZ Management himself directly. My Supervisor happened to already be at the gate and was present while that family was boarding. She noticed the bag looked different and asked me to take a look and immediately I knew that was prohibited on Company flights. My Supervisor was unsure but luckily Management sent out an email recently in regards to these type of bags and Company's policy. I was surprised my Supervisor wasn't aware of this and also was unsure of what the protocol is. The passengers ended up being deplaned and removed from the flight so that they can sort out how they will be able to still keep their bag without flying with it. I did explain to them Company's policy. I ended up rebooking the family of 3 for the next day. Per my Supervisor's request, she wanted to provide a hotel accommodation and meal vouchers. I did what she asked and sent it to the passengers. Another thing, is they flew from ZZZ on this same date and ZZZ must have not noticed this prohibited bag and allowed to connect with them to ZZZ2. Luckily I was there to intervene, and to ensure everyone's safety.
ASRSN:2176306.s: A flight attendant identified a prohibited rideable carry-on bag on ZZZ1 during boarding, noting the item had been missed by ZZZ staff on a prior connecting flight. The family of three was deplaned, rebooked for the next day, and provided hotel and meal vouchers per supervisor instruction.

ASRSN:2176310.n: While taxing on the Charlie line, in route to C21, with an air carrier aircraft in tow an employee bus crossed in front of our Tug, forcing us to hit the brakes.
ASRSN:2176310.s: While towing an air carrier aircraft on the Charlie line en route to C21, an employee bus crossed in front of the tug, forcing the crew to apply the brakes.

ASRSN:2176391.n: During the pre-departure phase of a departing 737 on gate XX yesterday at approximately XA50, while capturing the aircraft with the LEKTRO, the aircraft and LEKTRO rolled back approximately 3 feet due to the brake not being set on the LEKTRO. The driver was in the seat and unaware of the movement. The crew and I were able to prevent further movement and potential damage or injury by getting the driver's attention to stop. Afterwards I explained to the driver the need to set the brake every time when connecting to an aircraft.
ASRSN:2176391.s: During pre-departure of a 737, the aircraft and LEKTRO rolled back 3 feet because the driver failed to set the vehicle brake. The crew and reporter alerted the driver to stop the movement, preventing potential damage or injury.

ASRSN:2176396.n: I was seated in the tractor with my trainer seated right next to me. We heard a clink and realized the towbar had disconnected from the nosegear and I immediately told the brakerider 'breakaway set brakes'. The scene was frozen and management and maintenance were notified immediately.
ASRSN:2176396.s: A pilot and trainer in a tractor reported a towbar disconnecting from the nosegear during a tow operation. The pilot immediately instructed the brakerider to set brakes, freezing the scene while management and maintenance were notified.

ASRSN:2176535.n: Approximately 1 hour before landing I was preparing to do the service in FC (First Class). I heard the fire alarm chime four times. I could also hear it in the cockpit. I immediately looked toward the FC LAV, no one was in there. I glanced at the BC (Business Class) LAV and noticed the occupied sign was green. The Captain called me on the interphone stating they have a fire alarm in the BC LAV. I headed toward that LAV to check. The #3 met me halfway into FC cabin and told me she thought the BC oven could be on fire. She explained that the #5 put the cookies in the oven and within a minute there was black smoke pouring out the oven vent in oven 5. She was adamant that there could be a fire in there and asked me (repeatedly) to not open the oven. I called the cockpit to tell them the situation. (That there could be a fire in the oven, but we didn't want to open the door to see.) The Captain explained he was about to [request priority handling] and needed to know if there were flames in the oven. I made sure that he wanted me to open the oven door. He did. I went back to the BC galley and told the #3 and #5 that the Captain needed me to open the oven door. #3 insisted that we do it with her holding a Halon extinguisher. She broke the seal and pulled the pin and on 3 I opened the oven door approximately 3 inches.What I saw-Thick black smoke.Charred oven racks.Burnt food.I did not see flame.I called the cockpit and told them. There were no flames, but everything was charred, and I believed that there had possibly been flames. I based it on what I saw and past experience of seeing burnt food. This looked more sever then past experiences. He said he was [requesting priority handling]. I ran through my briefing questions and was told we would not be evacuating but we had 10 minutes to secure the cabin for landing in ZZZ. I asked him if he was going to make an announcement, or should I? He stated he would make announcement after they went through their checklist. The checklist took a long time and as I was preparing the FC cabin for landing it was hard not explaining to the passengers why we were landing in ZZZ. The Captain made the announcement explaining we were landing in ZZZ and said preparefor landing. I turned the lights to bright (and left them that way). We secured the cabin and took our jump seats. I did my review. We landed and taxied to the gate. Shortly after we were told it was safe to continue on and we left.The following is how we decided as a team to err on the side of caution.The smoke was so thick that it was able to trigger the fire alarm through closed BC LAV door. We could smell smoke throughout the BC and FC cabin and were later told they could smell in the cockpit. My previous experiences with burnt food were dramatically different from what the oven looked like and smelled like when I looked inside. The #5 had used the oven for the meal service and there had been no smoke from that oven which led me and the crew to believe that it was possibly an electrical fire.Suggestions: Put a guard on heating element in oven to protect from food starting a fire.
ASRSN:2176535.s: Cabin crew reported thick black smoke and charred food from a Business Class oven, triggering fire alarms and causing the Captain to request priority handling. The aircraft landed safely at ZZZ after the crew secured the cabin, with the reporter suspecting an electrical fire due to the severity of the smoke.

ASRSN:2176537.n: When we got on the plane smelled like rotten eggs. Main cabin crew went to the back to set up then the number made a PA that we needed to get off the airplane. Said it was a fume incident. We advised the Captain and all got off the plane. Called Maintenance Supervisor and they came over to see us and they called paramedics. We each had to call medical support and we were told to get fresh air and to not fly but go to the hotel and take a shower and rinse out our eyes.
ASRSN:2176537.s: Cabin crew reported a rotten egg smell and a fume incident on the aircraft, prompting an evacuation. Maintenance and paramedics responded, advising the crew to seek fresh air, shower, and refrain from flying.

ASRSN:2176604.n: I taxied for takeoff and checked the windsock. It indicated a slight south wind. I pulled up AWOS and confirmed about 3 knots from a southerly direction. I announced on the radio my intention to depart south. I did not hear any radio traffic, so I proceeded to my run up and then announced departure on runway XX, straight out. I checked for traffic and observed no one downwind or base and took off. As I rotated and climbed out I saw an airplane just touching down in the opposite direction runway XY. I looked at my radio and realized I had not switched from AWOS to CTAF so none of my radio calls had been heard and an airplane had entered the pattern unbeknownst to me.My error was the failure to switch to the proper CTAF frequency so anyone in the pattern knew my intentions and scanning the pattern more thoroughly to the south for possible traffic. The correct action is to verify and ensure you are on CTAF at all times during taxi, run up and takeoff, listen for traffic and confirm intentions of all traffic within and approaching the traffic pattern.
ASRSN:2176604.s: The pilot departed runway XX southbound without switching from AWOS to CTAF, failing to hear or announce intentions to an aircraft landing on opposite runway XY. The incident resulted from the pilot's error in not verifying the correct frequency and insufficient traffic scanning.

ASRSN:2176606.n: In the traffic pattern at ZZZ practicing short approaches. When I realized we were too low, I decided to convert the power-off 180 into a normal landing, by stopping the descent rate and adding power to get back onto glide path. We were coming over the threshold, I added power to get back onto glide path, then took power out once we were established in the flare. We were in a very nose pitch high attitude, and I was struggling to push the nose down, then the CFI took over controls, added full power to initiate a go around and wasn't able to push the elevator down either. He went power idle, and was able to force the elevator down, we safely landed on the runway. But, we only had less than 1,000 ft of runway left, so we went off the end of the runway, maintaining centerline, into the gravel. After we shut the plane down and exited safely, we noticed a piece of the stabilizer was lodged in between the stabilizer and the elevator, essentially locking it into place. The right main gear tire was also flat, possibly popped during the landing. There was no major structural damage to the aircraft, from what we examined. Neither one of us, student and instructor, sustained any injuries.
ASRSN:2176606.s: A student and CFI in a training aircraft at ZZZ went off the runway end into gravel after a stuck elevator prevented a go-around during a short approach. The elevator was locked by a stabilizer piece, causing a high nose attitude and flat tire, though no injuries or major structural damage occurred.

ASRSN:2176616.n: I was flying from ZZZ to ZZZ1 in a Mooney. At ZZZ1 runway XX was closed so I was landing on the shorter runway XY. Though it was VMC, I chose to use the RNAV XY to make it easier to find the airport and for a more controlled landing.I watched my speed carefully so as to not float too far down the runway. The runway begins uphill on the XY end.The plane came down hard, and nose wheel first and I had a prop strike. The nose wheel structure was damaged. I was able to taxi, but when I went to turn onto the taxiway, I could not turn sharp enough to make the turn. As a result, I had to be towed to parking. The airport was closed for about 10 minutes until the tow got to me.Mechanics came and inspected the airplane. They confirmed the damage to the nose wheel struts/structure and the bent propeller. The airplane was left at ZZZ1.My understanding is that this incident does not count as an NTSB accident and does not need to be reported to them.In the future, I will be more careful not to allow my airspeed to drop below what is appropriate (75 knots) on short final and to use aggressive power if it does drop below that. Also, on uphill runways, I will leave some power on until I am a couple feet off the ground.
ASRSN:2176616.s: The pilot of a Mooney landing on uphill Runway XY at ZZZ1 experienced a hard nose-wheel-first touchdown and propeller strike due to low airspeed. The resulting nose gear damage prevented taxiing, requiring a tow to parking and leaving the aircraft at the airport.

ASRSN:2176619.n: While in cruise enroute to ZZZ1 engine suddenly began to run extremely rough. Quick diagnosis and troubleshooting resulted in no changes to performance (Mix, fuel pump, prop and throttle adjustment) or roughness. XXXX was squawked with immediate south bound turn towards closest support of ZZZ. Immediate delegation and diversion due to mountains to north and rising terrain straight ahead. ZZZ ATC contacted with [a request for priority handling], airport in site. CTAF advised inbound Runway XX inbound traffic. Landed RWY XX, taxi to ramp and shut off. Upon inspection by A&P onsite found to be a bad Left Mag.
ASRSN:2176619.s: The pilot experienced severe engine roughness in cruise due to a faulty left magneto, which troubleshooting could not resolve. The aircraft was diverted to ZZZ for a priority landing on Runway XX after ATC coordination and terrain avoidance.

ASRSN:2176628.n: I executed an emergency maneuver at the time of this event to avoid a mid air collision with aircraft Y. I was on an IFR approach into PWT flying the RNAV 20 approach and under the care of Seattle Approach. I was assigned and flying at altitude 3000. There were two things happening at the time of my frequency change to 120.1. ATC had advised regarding the incoming traffic, but I had not yet made vision contact with Aircraft X. I was keeping an eye on this traffic and wondering why it was flying directly to the GITRE waypoint which is exactly where I predicted we would converge at approximately the same altitude. At about the Lemolo location, I received an urgent traffic alert on my Garmin TFC screen and instinctively maneuvered to avoid this traffic while keeping an eye on it on the ADS-B chart. I had no time to notify ATC of my altitude change but was in the midst of an emergency avoidance maneuver to climb to the right to avoid aircraft X in traffic.After analyzing the data online the data clearly shows that had I continued on my present heading with no immediate traffic avoidance instructions from ATC, the two aircraft would have met head on with no more than 200' of separation assuming that everyone's instruments were reporting faithfully.I do not understand why ATC did not vector me around this traffic and as a practical matter why this aircraft was flying outbound on the IFR instrument approach procedure (presumably on a VFR flight).ATC questioned why I had not requested an altitude change. My assessment is that in the heat of the moment, I needed to avoid the imminent collision and that was the only action I was taking first. In retrospect, I might have keyed the logbook deferral sheet (list) and notified ATC that I was executing an emergency avoidance maneuver. But we have always been taught (Aviation, Navigate, Communicate) and in this case, as pilot in command, my only action was to avoid what was rapidly becoming a midair collision course.
ASRSN:2176628.s: The pilot executing an RNAV 20 IFR approach into PWT at 3,000 feet performed an emergency climb to the right to avoid a head-on collision with Aircraft X. The pilot attributed the near-miss to a lack of ATC vectors and prioritized immediate avoidance over communication due to the imminent threat.

ASRSN:2176632.n: I am a Jump Pilot flying a Twin Otter out of ZZZ conducting skydive operations. at XA:08, during my climb up to altitude, an A319 flew directly underneath me about 400 ft below my position, I didn't know about it until after he was already passed me. there were no warnings from ATC, and when I asked them about the traffic they mentioned the aircraft was talking on a different frequency. During my descent I called up the Center frequency the A319 was talking to, and the controller said that the aircraft was talking to another controller, therefore no resolutions were made. Looking at the ATC recordings I've found that the A319 flying into ZZZ1 was vectored off of the ZZZZZ X arrival flying southbound, and then was cleared direct to ZZZZZ1, which, henceforth flew the A319 through the ZZZ Skydive Area and directly underneath me.
ASRSN:2176632.s: A Jump Pilot in a Twin Otter reported an A319 passed 400 feet below during climb at ZZZ without ATC warning. The A319 was vectored through the skydive area due to clearance changes and frequency separation, preventing conflict resolution.

ASRSN:2176633.n: I was departing Runway five at ISO en route to ZZZ which requires a left turn and an aircraft was entering the left downwind for Runway 5. ISO Tower told me that I could take my left turn to ZZZ too early and the other aircraft descended into the downwind as I ascended to my cruising altitude. The other aircraft would not stop descending into the downwind and used ZERO radio calls or ADM to see/navigate away from me on the ADS-B. I saw his icon go from +04 (400 ft above me) all the way to +01, and I called Kinston Tower to tell them I had traffic converging and he almost disrespectfully told me to take evasive action absolutely not aware of how close this could have been to a double fatality. The only reason it was not is because I pitched the nose down and started descending away from the converging aircraft which brought my airspeed into the yellow at about 130 kts. while I was around 800-900 feet above the surface. Complacency from both the other pilot and controller caused this, at the end of the day it is the pilot's responsibility to make responsible and safe ADM, and that was not done at all and my evasive action is the reason I am typing this and not in the news for an aircraft collision. I got zero alert from the TCAS but I used the ADS-B altitude reporting to take this action.
ASRSN:2176633.s: The pilot departing Runway 5 at ISO reported a near-collision with an aircraft on left downwind after Tower cleared an early turn. The pilot executed evasive descent to 130 knots at 800–900 feet AGL using ADS-B data, attributing the incident to controller and other pilot complacency.

ASRSN:2176646.n: We had been having problems with the fuel cap on the L wing of this aircraft and were heading to ZZZ from ZZZ1 for repairs. We planned to keep the fuel low since we knew repairs to the tank or tanks was going to take place. We were at ZZZ discussing the cap and several other maintenance issues with the mechanic. Myself and the CFI candidate student became distracted and did not check fuel leaving ZZZ which we should have done since out mission changed. Take off from ZZZ, climb, and cruise were normal. The engine sputtered minutes after we exited Class Delta airspace. We checked fuel tanks, engine kept idling, but would not produce power. We turned north and we landed with a left quartering tailwind on a county road - cross/tail wind was about 12-15 knots from the west/south west and we landed on the dirt road heading about north. This was the closest landing area without wires or obvious obstacles. We did land hard, but safely. We called the mechanics at ZZZ and he brought us fuel - about 28 gallons. We pumped it into the R tank, started up, and took off to the south on the dirt road because the wind had shifted slightly and the road was sloping downward to the south. I flew without the student back to ZZZ and had a normal landing without incident. Had we doubled checked the fuel at ZZZ and refueled, the off airport landing would not have been necessary. Distractions, lack of focus, being in a hurry, and a complete pre-flight could have prevented this issue from happening.
ASRSN:2176646.s: The pilot and student departed ZZZ with insufficient fuel due to distraction during maintenance discussions, causing engine power loss shortly after exiting Class Delta airspace. They executed a safe off-airport landing on a county road, refueled, and returned to ZZZ without further incident.

ASRSN:2176654.n: My wingman and I flew VFR into ALM from in 2 military aircraft. We made 20NM, 10NM, 3NM, downwind, base, and short final CTAF calls for a left visual overhead break for RWY 22. After landing roll-out, I made an 'Alamogordo traffic, Aircraft X back taxi runway 22' call on 122.8. As I began my back taxi, a light twin flew overhead my wingman and me at approximately 150 feet while we were still on the active runway. The pilot of the twin stated, 'A back taxi call would have been nice.' I replied, 'Sir, we made a call on CTAF.' The twin pilot stated, 'I did not hear it on VHF. Have a great time.' I replied, 'Sir, a back taxi call was absolutely made.' No further communication between me and the twin pilot occurred. The pilot of the twin should have never released his brakes until he heard a Aircraft X clear of the active call on CTAF. The airfield has NOTAMS and AWOS stating that Taxiway work is in progress and that Taxiway A is closed between Taxiway D and A4 with barricades in place. There is no place to exit runway 22 once past midfield, all pilots flying at ALM should know that. I turned around at approximately the 2 board (7000 feet from the departure end), and the twin pilot should have easily seen two aircraft still on the runway. The aircraft made all appropriate CTAF calls. The pilot of the twin not only had a runway incursion but also created an extremely unsafe situation by departing a runway while aircraft were still on it. He could have easily collided with the aircraft if he didn't have the thrust available to climb or if he aborted his takeoff once on the roll.Of note - the tail number was given to us by others at the airport, who saw the event happen as they watched us land from the ramp directly adjacent to where the incident happened. We are lucky that the twin pilot had the ability to climb at the rate he did, given the airport elevation of 4200 feet. Had the pilot chosen to abort, I do not assess he would have had enough runway to stop on the runway before colliding with us. The twin pilot displayed reckless behavior, poor judgment, and a nonchalant attitude post overflying us.
ASRSN:2176654.s: Two military VFR aircraft back-taxied Runway 22 at ALM after landing while a light twin departed the active runway at 150 feet. The reporter attributes the runway incursion and unsafe situation to the twin pilot's failure to verify the runway was clear before takeoff, despite the military aircraft making CTAF calls.

ASRSN:2176667.n: Had power loss while in cruise and RPM's dropped did my checklist procedure and when I pushed the mixture in it almost lost all power so mixture was put back to lean and power came back partially tried to switch to single tanks and almost lost full power on each tank then it was switched to both all that while losing altitude then we glided other plane to the airport ZZZ with partial power and notified the school.
ASRSN:2176667.s: The pilot experienced partial power loss and altitude loss during cruise due to fuel mixture and tank selection issues. After restoring partial power by selecting both tanks, the aircraft glided to airport ZZZ with reduced power.

ASRSN:2176670.n: Our airplane was holding short of Runway XXR at Taxiway 1, per ZZZ Tower's instruction. After a short period of time, the pilot monitoring and I believe we heard the Tower Controller clear our airplane to line up and wait Runway XXR. The pilot monitoring replied to the Tower Controller on the Tower frequency with our tail number and that we would line up and wait Runway XXR. Just after advancing our airplane over the hold short lines, the pilot monitoring and I noticed another airplane on the opposing taxiway in front of us taxiing past its respective hold short lines onto Runway XXR. I immediately took evasive action by depressing the brakes and bringing our airplane to a complete, safe, and abrupt stop. A near collision was not a factor here, our aircraft had only moved a few feet past the hold short lines before stopping. The pilot monitoring immediately asked the Tower Controller to confirm whether the line up and wait clearance was for our tail number. The Tower Controller replied negative. The pilot monitoring asked the Tower Controller for further instructions on how we should proceed provided the current situation and our position. Now clear of the opposing airplane as it taxied into position for takeoff, the controller instructed our crew to taxi straight ahead off Runway XXR, make a three-hundred sixty degree turn, and hold short of Runway XXR. We immediately complied. Reflecting upon this event, the pilot monitoring and I believe we heard that our tail number had been cleared to line up and wait Runway XXR. Additionally, after the pilot monitoring replied to the Tower Controller that our tail number was cleared to line up and wait Runway XXR, the Tower Controller never corrected our read back, had it been erroneous. The Tower Controller may have actually said that the tail number of the opposing airplane was cleared to line up and wait Runway XXR. As both airplanes had taxied past the respective hold short lines, I noticed the other airplane had a similar tail number to ours. While it is understandable that confirmation bias and/or lack of absolute radio clarity may have led the pilot monitoring and I to believe the Tower Controller said our tail number, there are some things that could have changed the outcome of this event. First, our crew should slow down and ensure and actively agree with each other that we heard the full clearance for our tail number. Second, we should be more situationally aware that there was another airplane of the same type on the opposing taxiway and that it may have a similar call sign. As a result of this, I completed a WINGS course about preventing runway incursions to be better educated as a pilot. It is also now more thoroughly engrained in me that if uncertain of any part of an instruction, stop and ask ATC. ATC may not be able to immediately correct an erroneous read back if, as an example, they are prioritizing something else. Further, I recognize that both pilots and controllers make mistakes, and it is our collective duty to be proactive with mitigating and eliminating mistakes. I appreciate all the hard work our ATC controllers do every day to keep everyone safe.
ASRSN:2176670.s: The flight crew mistakenly believed they were cleared to line up and wait on Runway XXR due to a similar tail number and radio clarity issues, causing them to cross hold short lines. They stopped safely after seeing another aircraft enter the runway, and ATC confirmed the clearance was not for them, instructing the crew to exit and re-hold.

ASRSN:2176674.n: My student, Person A, was conducting his third solo flight to the local area. He proceeded back to the airport, ZZZ, and successfully accomplished a landing. On the second and final landing, he began a stabilized approach to runway XXL on proper speed of approximately 70 kts. I witnessed the round out and flare from the ground which looked to be in the proper landing attitude. Upon touchdown the aircraft began to porpoise and proceeded to drift off the right side of the runway. All solo endorsements were proper completed and student document verified before flight. I have flown with this student many times in the last few weeks and observed no issues with landing technique. Prior to this flight I briefed the student on proper crosswind technique should one arise and procedures for go around and bad landing recovery. At the time of the occurance, there was a slight crosswind of only a few knots and was endorsed up to 10 kts as I have witnessed proper crosswind proficiency with this student.
ASRSN:2176674.s: A student pilot conducting a solo landing at ZZZ on runway XXL drifted off the right side after porpoising on touchdown. The instructor reported the approach was stabilized with proper speed and attitude, attributing the incident to an unexplained loss of control despite a slight crosswind.

ASRSN:2176676.n: Cessna 172During the preflight inspection, we didn't see any leaks or any abnormalities from the brake system. --- Brake check before starting taxiing Pilot Flying has full brake authority (normal).Pilot monitoring, left brake full authority, right brake soft --- During taxi, PF was taxiing without any issues. We were down taxiway 1 from spot XX in a straight line.I took the controls before steering right on taxiway 1, but before the turn, I gave controls to PF, and we did not have any side, not PF nor PM right brake authority to maintain the airplane on the centerline while the turn, and we skidded off of the shoulder of the taxiway. The airplane was towed.
ASRSN:2176676.s: Pilots of a Cessna 172 lost right brake authority during a taxi turn on Taxiway 1, causing the aircraft to skid off the shoulder. The plane was subsequently towed after the crew could not maintain the centerline despite normal preflight brake checks.

ASRSN:2176677.n: I was talking to Buffalo Approach on 121.0 and heard other aircraft talking with Cincinnati Approach (both sides), also on 121.0. I reported this to Buffalo Approach, and they replied that's a common problem with both Cincinnati and Toronto, depending on the weather. This sector needs a different frequency that doesn't overlap with other sectors so near by.
ASRSN:2176677.s: A pilot reported hearing Cincinnati Approach communications on the shared 121.0 MHz frequency while contacting Buffalo Approach. Buffalo Approach attributed the overlap to weather conditions, prompting the pilot to recommend a dedicated frequency to prevent interference with nearby sectors.

ASRSN:2176698.n: Please note that this is per my best recollection. My intention is not to cause any trouble for any party, as the solution was resolved positively. My goal is to simply inform of how I as a pilot will respond to this in the future. The goal of this flight was a time building flight for cross country hours for my instrument rating via Part 61. I had VFR flight following from ZZZ1 and was handed off from ZZZ Approach to ZZZ Tower. I was a little nervous about this flight as it was the first time I had flown solo to the field. I informed Tower that I was 10 miles inbound touch and go, with a departure to south to follow. I was instructed to contact at 3 miles out and plan for a left downwind for Runway XX. This approach different from the other flight I'd done to ZZZ, which was on the larger Runway XY/XZ. I was approaching from near due south (northbound heading toward ZZZ). As I neared the 3 mile distance from the field, immediately prior to informing Tower that I was at 3 miles, per requested, Tower preemptively informed me to enter a left downwind Runway XX. Rather than enquire if they are instructing me to do so immediately, or simply advising of how they want me to fly the pattern, I read back my instructions and entered a left downwind for Runway XX. This resulted in a wider traffic pattern than I am typically used to flying - and one that is a bigger than what the FAA airplane flying handbook recommends. I had the field in sight, though terrain features and the condition of Runway XX made it much more difficult to consistently make out relative to the larger Runway XZ at a 3 mile distance. I was advised of other traffic in the approach phase for Runway XX, which split my visual duties between maintaining visual contact with Runway XX and visual contact with other traffic. Abeam XX I began my descent below traffic pattern altitude and turned base following landing traffic on a 4 mile final. Tower then radioed me and told me to turn base, which caused confusion as I felt I was already on a base leg (cross checking with my HSI (Horizontal Situation Indicator) and GPS extended runway centerline confirmed this). Tower informed me that I had descended below traffic pattern altitude of 1600 feet - which cross checked with my altimeter - however I realized I must have been too low for the distance of my (extended) base leg from the runway (altitude was approximately 1200 feet MSL). At this point the instructions I received from Tower did not fully align with my expectations of a stabilized approach. While I felt that I had Runway XX in sight - I informed Tower that I wished to abandon the approach and try again, that I was new to the area, and that I had lost consistent visual contact with Runway XX (I still had contact with the runway, but the information I was receiving from Tower made me doubt that I had full situational awareness of where my plane was approaching...if it was the correct runway or if I had some sort of expectation bias going on. Something just didn't add up). Shortly following this request, Tower inquired if I could see the approach end of the Runway XX - which I said yes - I had just then watched another plane touch down on Runway XX confirming that my approach was indeed pointing at the correct runway. He asked if I made a right 270 across XX's final if I would be able to descend and land - which I said yes. I was cleared for a right 270, lined up with XX's final, and performed a touch and go. I thanked Tower for helping me regain situational awareness and departed the area with an uneventful trip back to my home field.This root cause of this situation occurred when I entered a downwind leg 3 miles from the field with further degradation to situational awareness and confidence in a stabilized approach occurring as the approach continued. This caused confusion on my end as I had to work harder to maintain a 100% positive visual identification with Runway XX while also looking for traffic at a distance further than usual. In the moment, it felt as though ATC had instructed me to enter a downwind leg at a 3 mile distance from the field, but the reality is that they were instructing me to enter a normal downwind leg (and that instruction came when I was at the 3 mile mark from the airport). In the future - I intend to ask for clarification from ATC as soon as I feel I receive an instruction that does not align with the norm (entering a larger traffic pattern, for example). ATC did an excellent job identifying that my approach had momentarily shown signs of slipping from a stabilized criteria.
ASRSN:2176698.s: A solo student pilot conducting a touch-and-go at ZZZ entered an unusually wide downwind leg at 3 miles, causing confusion and a descent below 1600 feet. The pilot aborted the approach due to lost situational awareness but successfully completed a touch-and-go after ATC clarified instructions and confirmed runway alignment.

ASRSN:2176724.n: i was being vectored for the rnav XX approach into ZZZ. approach said turn 270 maintain 1600 till established cleared rnav XX approach as i was turning to intercept the final approach course i was shy of ZZZZZ , which is 1600ft crossing, i inadvertently descended to 1300ft, atc told me i am at 1300 climb to 1600 till established and gave me an altimeter setting . i was established on the final approach course but was not across ZZZZZ at the time i immediately climbed to 1600 till i crossed ZZZZZ then was told to contact tower i called tower and they cleared me to land. As i was told to turn to 270 that would of put me left of course so i was heading to intercept the final approach course as i visually saw runway straight ahead i was not realizing i was at 1300ft shy of ZZZZZ intersection when told by atc to climb to 1600 i did so asap. i should have realized i was not at ZZZZZ just yet before descending.
ASRSN:2176724.s: The pilot inadvertently descended to 1,300 feet while intercepting the RNAV XX approach, failing to maintain the required 1,600-foot crossing altitude at the ZZZZZ intersection. Air Traffic Control instructed an immediate climb to 1,600 feet, which the pilot executed before crossing the fix and receiving landing clearance.

ASRSN:2176733.n: After conducting a training demonstration, the sUAS was landed in a stationary position on a ground control point (helipad). The sUAS was powered off and no batteries were installed at the time of the collision. The sUAS, while on a clearly marked landing zone and with present people on notice of drone operations being conducted, was run over by a fire department vehicle. The drone was destroyed beyond repair and was rendered a total loss. Only the drone sustained damage and no external damage was noted to any buildings, vehicles, or other notable items. Furthermore, no injuries occurred during the event.The purpose of this report is for documentation purposes.
ASRSN:2176733.s: A stationary, powered-off sUAS on a marked helipad was run over by a fire department vehicle after a training demonstration. The drone was destroyed beyond repair, but no injuries or damage to other vehicles or buildings occurred.

ASRSN:2176734.n: I was unaware of the requirements to fly in this area and to fly a UAS, in general. That day I went home and started reading up on the requirements and determined that I did not have the correct registration, waivers, etc. I have since gotten my TRUST certificate, registered my UAS with the FAA and enrolled in a part 107 course. I intend to apply for the part 107 and in that course I learned about this reporting procedure. I stopped the learning module and immediately came here to self-report the incident.
ASRSN:2176734.s: A UAS operator reported flying without required registration or waivers due to unawareness of regulations. The operator subsequently obtained a TRUST certificate, registered the UAS, and enrolled in a Part 107 course to ensure future compliance.

ASRSN:2176735.n: Flying an experimental aircraft departing on Runway XX, I made a normal takeoff. Wind at ground level was estimated at 6 to 8 kts from east, gusting to perhaps 12 to 15 kts. No wind socks were available as they had been taken down a few days earlier in anticipation of Hurricane. Rotation was about 65 kts, and I began a normal climb to approximately tree top level where I was hit by a surprisingly hard gust from right side rolling the aircraft hard to left. I countered with hard right aileron. I made a mistake when struggling to fight the turbulence, I took my right hand (dominate hand) off the throttle and put it on top of the control stick to assist the left hand. In the process, I inadvertently activated the 'coolie hat' causing the pitch trim to move to the maximum nose down. I was doing my best to crush the control stick for several seconds. Also having neglected the throttle for several seconds, it had crept out about 1 inch significantly reducing thrust, but I failed to notice the reduced power. I slammed into the ground, wings level but slightly nose down attitude, causing a bounce back into the air. The aircraft did not stall. A glance at the IAS showed something over 70 kts so I elected to go around. Restoring power added airspeed but not climb rate. I was in still moderate turbulence and not climbing normally with no unpopulated space to make a safe landing. I struggled to stay in the air. Trimmed full nose down, pulling as hard as I could, I could not raise the nose more than a degree or two above the horizon. I flew over the residential community north of the airport at a low altitude (estimated at 80 to 100 feet AGL), with barely enough altitude to avoid obstacles. As soon as possible, I turned west to get over a less populated area and was able to climb to perhaps 300 feet AGL where the turbulence abated to a less frightening level and trimmed for nose up. Climbing through about 1100 feet AGL, I entered an area of light turbulence. I was shaken and chose to go to a nearby paved airport which has no trees and a runway more into the winds. After landing, I measured the full down limit for down pitch and found that the trim tab had traveled more than 10 inches beyond its designated limit. I did not build this experimental aircraft but purchased it with 70 hours time on it. The down elevator had not been set to proper travel range. I am in the process of modifying the trim system to limit travel to the point where it can be overpowered by the pilot when needed. The aircraft sustained a broken nose wheel pant but no other damage. No one was hurt.
ASRSN:2176735.s: The pilot of an experimental aircraft encountered severe turbulence during initial climb, inadvertently activating a malfunctioning pitch trim that moved to maximum nose down. This caused a ground impact and a low-altitude go-around, but the pilot safely landed at another airport after discovering the trim tab exceeded its travel limits.

ASRSN:2176745.n: While on autopilot and descending on the arrival, the aircraft suddenly rolled right to approximately 40 degrees of bank. The PM (FO) announced 'UPSET;' and I disconnected the autopilot and gently rolled the aircraft back to wings level. The PM informed ATC of the action as it caused us to slightly veer off track. We attributed it to the wake turbulence of an aircraft that had just crossed our path. This was reported to ATC, as well. We checked on the FAs who reported no injuries or impact from the event. We continued to a normal landing. While flying straight and level with the autopilot on, the aircraft unexpectedly rolled to the right to approximately 40 degrees of bank. FO (PM) called 'upset', CA (PF) immediately disconnected the autopilot and corrected the flight attitude back to straight and level flight. The PF (CA) continued hand flying to an uneventful landing.
ASRSN:2176745.s: During an arrival descent on autopilot, the aircraft unexpectedly rolled right to 40 degrees, attributed by the crew to wake turbulence. The Captain disconnected the autopilot, corrected the attitude, and hand-flew to a normal landing with no injuries reported.

ASRSN:2176764.n: We were given a visual approach to Runway 28L. Approach Control paired us with a 757 which we were faster than, given 180 kt. to bridge. As soon as we changed to Tower they told us to slow to final approach speed. They put Aircraft Z on the runway and cleared them for takeoff. No sooner did they do that they cleared an Aircraft A heavy to line up and wait. Told him we were on a 4-mile final, barely cleared them for takeoff. As we continued approaching runway, we at 200 ft., they were just starting to rotate. We had a lot of wash from the double heavy takeoffs. FO did job of correcting and landing plane. A miss would have been mess with a plane on the right, a heavy that just took off, and a heavy rotating. No reason for the spacing issue that was created by the Tower.
ASRSN:2176764.s: Tower cleared a heavy aircraft to line up and wait while the reporting aircraft was on a 4-mile final, resulting in a close call at 200 feet with wake turbulence from two preceding heavy takeoffs. The First Officer corrected the flight path for a safe landing, though the reporter attributed the unsafe spacing entirely to Tower errors.

ASRSN:2176776.n: On our descent into ZZZ, the right engine rolled back. We were approximately at 16000 ft when the engine rolled back. The Captain ran the QRC and I [advised ATC]. We landed safely on Runway XXR and had personal inspect the aircraft before taxing to the gate. Descending thru 16,000 right engine failed. Performed the engine failure QRC and QRH. Landed safely on runway XXR, cleared runway and stopped. Personnel performed inspection of aircraft, found nothing abnormal. Taxied to the gate.
ASRSN:2176776.s: During descent into ZZZ at 16,000 ft, the right engine rolled back and failed. The crew executed the engine failure QRC and QRH, landed safely on Runway XXR, and taxied to the gate after a normal inspection found no abnormalities.

ASRSN:2176881.n: Upon liftoff and calling for gear up, the left engine driven hydraulic pump failed. Pressure was low on both the engine and electric pumps until the gear had fully cycled. We asked for delayed vectors to assess the situation. It was decided to return to ZZZ. QRH procedure was run and after a short delay to get everything in order, and we returned to ZZZ with a visual approach to XXC backed up with the ILS. The approach and landing were normal. Fire rescue followed us to the gate and there was no need of additional services. Flight ABCD ZZZ-ZZZ1 was a Linecheck, during the event decisions were made by the captain with the participation and help of the FO, and the Checkairman. I was monitoring and the FO flying, we departed runway XXR, during gear retraction the Left Engine hydraulic pump low pressure light came on, we notified departure control of having a mechanical issue and requested radar vectors to remain in the terminal area and 10 thousand feet. We ran the QRH for Hydraulic Pump Low Pressure which instructed to turn the affected pump off. The electric hydraulic pump maintained pressure in the system and there was no sign of leak. I contacted maintenance who gave us a frequency for Maintenance Control. We tried calling several times but no answers. At that point we all agreed that the logical option was to return to the field. I instructed the FO to notify ATC of our intentions, ATC conveniently gave us priority. During that time I called Operations hoping they would coordinate our intentions with dispatch as well as find us a gate. They did provide the gate but told us to notify dispatch which I did via ACARS. I then notified the Cabin Crew that we were returning to the field, to expect a normal landing in the following 10 minutes, and to prepare the cabin for landing. It was followed by a PA to the passengers. I took the controls and the FO briefed the approach. We had priority the FO landed runway XXC, we obtained short taxi instructions to cross XXR followed by ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) vehicles. safety vehicles followed us to the gate. Approaching gate 1 the DGS (Docking Guidance System) system failed with emergency authority and well clear of obstacles I parked the aircraft with the guidance of a single marshaller.Engine 1 hydraulic pump failure. It ended up being a stressful situation, it was day 4 of the trip we were tired from the short 10 hour the night prior and while having a linecheck on that last turn, the pressure of having one of my piers onboard evaluating while the event took place. You can't help but get affected by that.
ASRSN:2176881.s: During a linecheck departure, the left engine-driven hydraulic pump failed, causing low pressure until gear retraction completed. The crew returned to ZZZ for a normal landing with fire rescue escort after following QRH procedures and coordinating with ATC and maintenance.

ASRSN:2176893.n: After engaging TOGA for takeoff, the autothrottles failed to set the correct N1. This issue was promptly identified, and a rejected takeoff was performed at a low speed of 83 knots. We returned to the gate and completed the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook (AML) write-up for maintenance.
ASRSN:2176893.s: The pilot rejected takeoff at 83 knots after autothrottles failed to set correct N1 following TOGA engagement. The aircraft returned to the gate, and the issue was documented in the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook.

ASRSN:2176897.n: Just prior to reaching the waypoint ZZZZZ at 31000 ft, during a lavatory break, while I was reentering the flight deck, the autopilot disengaged and the aircraft started to descend and turn. This was caused by a IRU failure (as indicated by an IRU FAULT light and associated Cautions from systems dependent on heading and altitude from the IRU). We lost heading and attitude information on the CA (Captain)primary display and heading on the standby ADI. The CA took control of the aircraft from the minor upset and brought the aircraft back up to the cleared altitude. The aircraft descended approximately 550 ft below our cleared altitude during the event. We ran the associated QRH checklist for the IRU fault and recovered attitude and heading to the CA side using the IRS Transfer Switch. During the failure, the heading and wind information on the Nav displays appeared to be inaccurate, so we coordinated with ATC for confirmation of our heading and position relative to our flight plan course, and advised them of our equipment failure. ATC descended us below RVSM airspace and we continued to our destination. ATC advised that they did not have an indication of our altitude deviation. Over time the Nav displays and wind information eventually became reliable. We decided that it would be better that the FO land the aircraft due to the loss of flight director guidance on the CA side. The approach and landing was hand flown to ZZZ in accordance with the QRH without further incident. Cause: Equipment failure appears to be the cause. No recommendations to mitigate risk.
ASRSN:2176897.s: During cruise at 31,000 ft, an IRU failure caused autopilot disengagement and a 550 ft descent below cleared altitude. The Captain recovered the aircraft, ATC descended them below RVSM airspace, and the First Officer hand-flew the landing due to lost flight director guidance.

ASRSN:2176902.n: Departing out of ZZZ on the ZZZZZ4 Departure, the flight director commanded a left turn instead of a right. The PM's flight director was indicating correctly and had me make a right turn to get back on course. He then selected heading. After we were on an intercept course the PM selected NAV mode and flight director began to indicate correctly. This was without making any changes to the FMS. No other issues were encountered. Cause: Continue to monitor aircraft automation and instruments. PM trapped the issue.
ASRSN:2176902.s: During departure on the ZZZZZ4 Departure, the pilot's flight director incorrectly commanded a left turn while the PM's indicated correctly. The PM manually selected heading to correct the course, and the system returned to normal after selecting NAV mode without FMS changes.

ASRSN:2176936.n: During the preflight Dangerous Goods (DG) inspection the FO noticed that there was a separation violation. There were DG pallets in positions 1L and 2L. Position 2L had incompatible items with a 1.4 in the front and a 3 in the aft. However, there was a 3 in the rear of the pallet in position 1L approximately 1 foot away from the 1.4 in position 2L.The FO brought it to my attention. We alerted the Supervisor, and requested that the DG staff fix this situation. After unloading the left side of the jet, they were able to rotate the pallet 180 degrees. This allowed all separation requirements to be met. This resulted in an approximate 40-minute delay in departure. No other complications were found.Cause: The DG staff were not taking in to account that these were pallets and not cans therefore what was in the fore pallet had to comply with the separation requirements of the aft pallet as well. 2 accessible Dangerous Goods (DG) pallets were loaded in 1L and 2L. During the DG inspection process I noted multiple separation requirements within each pallet. However, I noticed that the back" end of 1L pallet contains Class 3 and the "front" end of 2L pallet contains Class 1.4C. In other words, Class 1.4C and Class 3 are facing each other. Per the DG position summary, Class 1.4C requires separation from Class 3. While Class 3 and Class 1.4C were on different pallets, the separation requirement was not met (roughly a foot separation). DG staff was informed that the separation was acceptable and advised me accordingly after I raised my concern.I informed the Captain, which in return he contacted the Duty Officer and all of us were in agreement that the loading is not compliant. Ramp crew unloaded the left side on the main cargo deck and reloaded the DG in a compliant manner. That was accomplished by rotating pallet 2L 180 degrees resulting in Class 1.4C facing position 3L.Cause: Possible disconnect in communication between loading crew and DG staff.Suggestions: Vigilance and strong working knowledge is required from crew members / ramp agents / DG staff. When in doubt reach out and seek a definitive answer."
ASRSN:2176936.s: The First Officer identified a Dangerous Goods separation violation between Class 3 and Class 1.4C items on adjacent pallets 1L and 2L during preflight. Ramp crew rotated pallet 2L to correct the loading, causing a 40-minute departure delay due to DG staff misinterpreting pallet separation requirements.

ASRSN:2176947.n: As we are descending on a published arrival, to an altitude cleared by ATC (7400ft). A paraglider was in from of us. After me the PF saw and called it out, the Captain disconnected the autopilot, banked right and climbed to avoid a collision. The traffic came within 50-100ft from us. The area is not depicted as a glider area, the gliders are not required to have an ADS-B, ATC did not know of informed us of their presence in the area. The arrival procedure should have a note or depiction of the gliding area. As well as ATC should be informed of this activity. While on the ZIGGY8 arrival into Ontario between HITOP and NITIY, at or near the MVA of 7;400ft (as previously cleared down to by ATC) and at 250 kts, we had a near miss with a paraglider. We estimate the distance to be within 50-100ft. As the flying pilot I looked to my left to check the arrival chart on the iPad when the First Officer, the Pilot Monitoring, called out traffic. As collision was imminent, I immediately disconnected the autopilot, pulled hard right and climbed. The paraglider pilot, who was coming toward us in a right turn, appeared to pull hard right, accelerating his turn right. Passengers said they saw him go by the left side of the aircraft. Cause: Apparently there is a paraglider launch site in the area and it doesn't appear to be depicted on the IFR navigation charts. Suggestions: Please have ATC say, 'Use caution for paraglider/hang glider activity on the arrival', or something similar, to warn other pilots in the future. Educate the paraglider/hang glider pilots who use that launch site about the air traffic in the area.
ASRSN:2176947.s: During the ZIGGY8 arrival into Ontario at 7,400ft, the crew executed an emergency climb and right bank to avoid a paraglider within 50-100ft. The near miss occurred because the launch site is not depicted on charts, and ATC was unaware of the untracked glider activity.

ASRSN:2176979.n: The airplane was established in the landing configuration on the final approach with full flaps, and the before-landing checklist was completed. The student pilot was on the flight controls, attempting a short field landing on Runway XXL at ZZZ. The airplane crossed the threshold at approximately 80 feet AGL with an airspeed of 65 knots and touched down about 100 feet past the thousand-foot marker. Upon touchdown, slightly to the left of the runway, the student pilot reduced the wind correction and attempted to stop the aircraft by applying the brakes while trying to maintain the runway centerline using the right rudder. The aircraft began drifting to the right side of the runway. The student attempted to correct by applying left rudder to regain the centerline, at this point a tire noise was heard, caused by the tires skidding on the pavement. The instructor pilot immediately took over the flight controls and attempted to correct the airplane's drift. Rudder inputs were applied in an attempt to return to the runway centerline. However, the aircraft continued to drift and eventually exited the runway, turning 180 degrees around facing the approach end on Runway XXL. The aircraft came to a rest in the grass on the left side of the Runway XXL between [Taxiways] 1 and 2. The airplane was in a level position, with the right main landing gear and the nose landing gear in the grass, while the left main landing gear remained on the left edge of Runway XXL. After confirming that all occupants and the aircraft were safe, the instructor pilot successfully exited the runway. Once past the [Taxiway] 2 hold-short line, the instructor pilot contacted ATC for taxi instructions to the run-up area of XXL for a further exterior inspection of the aircraft.The aircraft was brought to a complete stop in the run-up area of XXL, where shutdown procedures were performed. The instructor pilot conducted a visual inspection of the airplane and found no visible damage. Airport operations personnel approached the aircraft for further inspection and confirmed that no damage was observed to the airport environment, runway, lights, or the aircraft.The airplane's engine was started again for a run-up performance check, which showed no noticeable deviations from standard. After confirming the aircraft was in safe condition, the instructor pilot requested taxi instructions from ATC to return to the FBO ramp. Instructions were given to taxi via 3-4 and hold short of Runway XXR. Clearance was then granted to cross Runway XXR and taxi via [taxiways] 5, 6, and 7 to the FBO ramp. After completing the shutdown procedures, the instructor pilot conducted another visual inspection of the airplane, again finding no noticeable damage. The instructor pilot then spoke with maintenance personnel, explaining the situation and requested a more in-depth inspection of the aircraft to ensure its airworthiness and safety.
